ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Cytogenetic disorders arise from chromosomal abnormalities that alter gene dosage or structure, causing developmental, metabolic, or oncologic problems. Clinicians must integrate family history, physical clues, and targeted tests to diagnose and manage these conditions.

sections.p: Cytogenetic disorders are caused by numerical or structural changes in chromosomes. They can be inherited or de novo and often present with recognizable physical features, developmental delay, or organ dysfunction.

Chromosomes carry genes; copy number or rearrangement changes alter gene expression. The phenotype depends on which genes are affected and whether the change is present in all cells (constitutional) or a subset (mosaic).
b: Copy number changes change gene dosage
Structural changes can disrupt gene function or create fusion genes

sections.p: The cell cycle and DNA repair pathways normally maintain chromosome integrity. Errors in replication, segregation, or repair lead to aneuploidy or rearrangements. Environmental factors (radiation, chemicals) can increase risk.
b: DNA double‑strand break misrepair causes translocations

sections.p: Abnormal chromosome number or structure leads to loss or gain of genes, disrupting developmental pathways. Common mechanisms include loss of tumor suppressor genes, gain of oncogenes, or dosage imbalance of developmental regulators.
b: Trisomy 21: extra copy of chromosome 21 genes
Deletion 22q11.2: loss of TBX1 and others

sections.p: Clinicians should suspect cytogenetic disorders when a patient has multiple congenital anomalies, growth retardation, or unexplained developmental delay. Early diagnosis guides surveillance for associated complications and genetic counseling.
b: Down syndrome: intellectual disability, heart defects, thyroid issues

t.b: Detects numerical and structural chromosomal abnormalities; abnormal result confirms diagnosis.
Targets specific loci; useful when karyotype is normal but a microdeletion is suspected.
Detects submicroscopic copy number changes; indicates deletions/duplications not seen on karyotype.
Identifies structural anomalies that may suggest chromosomal causes; guides need for invasive testing.

sections.p: Remember that many cytogenetic disorders are associated with increased maternal age and that some have specific physical stigmata. Use a systematic approach: history, exam, targeted testing, and counseling.
b: Maternal age >35 increases risk of trisomies

t.b: Screen for Down syndrome; abnormal result warrants diagnostic testing.
Look for dysmorphic features that point to specific syndromes.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe growth failure, unexplained developmental delay, multiple congenital anomalies, or family history of chromosomal disorders

faq.a: Most are lifelong; treatment focuses on managing complications and improving quality of life.

faq.q: Do all chromosomal abnormalities cause disease?
faq.a: Many are benign or have mild effects; severity depends on the genes involved and the extent of the abnormality.

faq.q: Is genetic counseling required for all families?
faq.a: Yes, to discuss recurrence risk, reproductive options, and implications for other family members.

exam: Explain why trisomy 21 leads to intellectual disability and congenital heart disease.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a newborn with cleft palate and cardiac defect.
Discuss management priorities for a patient with Klinefelter syndrome.
